title: The voice of another language
text: A good translation is a {{1}}: the reader must not notice it. That sounds like praise for invisibility, but the work behind it is {{2}}. The translator's first decisions are structural: where to break the sentences, whether to keep the original's long, winding periods or {{3}} them into the shorter ones the target language prefers. Then come the words without {{4}} — terms of address, food, swearing, class markers — where every solution is a compromise and the only fatal {{5}} is pretending that no compromise occurred. Humour is the {{6}} test: a pun rarely survives, so the translator must build a new joke in the same place, or accept the silence. Whether translation is creation or {{7}} has been argued since Cicero; the modern answer is that it is both, and that the translator's name belongs {{8}} the author's — a convention now printed on more and more title pages, to the quiet delight of a profession that has spent centuries invisible.

gaps.explanation: 'a good translation is a disguise' — it conceals itself; disgrace = shame, dispatch = a report or prompt sending.
'the work behind it is colossal' — vast in scale; colloquial = informal in speech.
'split them into the shorter ones' — divide them; spit = eject saliva, splurge = spend lavishly.
'words without equivalents' — no matching word in the other language; equilibrium = a state of balance.
'the only fatal error is pretending' — the deadly mistake; errand = a short trip on behalf of someone.
'humour is the ultimate test' — the final, hardest one; utter = complete ('utter nonsense'), untold = beyond counting.
'creation or copying' — the two candidate activities; cope takes 'with'.
'the translator's name belongs alongside the author's' — next to it; astride = with a leg each side, ajar = slightly open.
